title: scheduler: handle in-flight Pods with less memory
body: All cluster events during scheduling are piled up in inFlightEvents. The scheduler currently needs them to decide which queue should receive failed Pods, but recording every cluster event during a Pod's scheduling increases scheduler memory consumption, especially in a busy cluster. There may also be a memory leak around inFlightEvents. I want to reduce this memory impact as much as possible.

symptoms_visible: In a busy cluster, events occurring while Pods are being scheduled accumulate in inFlightEvents and increase scheduler memory consumption.
N0.label: N0 in-flight event memory concern reported

symptoms_visible: On my Kubernetes v1.30.3 cluster, the scheduler runs out of memory with QueueingHint enabled; after I disable that feature gate, it stops OOMing.
N1.label: N1 affected cluster reproduction established

symptoms_visible: The scheduler's memory continues growing, but it is still scheduling Pods.
We have encountered this on one cluster and I do not know what makes that case special.
N2.label: N2 profiles and runtime behavior collected

symptoms_visible: My debug logs show only about two to five in-flight Pods while the inFlightEvents count is already above 62,000 and keeps increasing.
N3.label: N3 unbounded event retention measured

symptoms_visible: With a temporary defer that calls Done for every ScheduleOne invocation, my debug output stays around one in-flight Pod and one in-flight event.
N3_x.label: N3_x unsafe unconditional cleanup probe

symptoms_visible: After testing the proposed multi-element-in-the-list change, the scheduler memory problem no longer occurs on my affected cluster.
N4.label: N4 robust candidate fix verified

symptoms_visible: With the multi-element in-flight tracking fix applied, the affected scheduler no longer accumulates inFlightEvents until it runs out of memory.
N_terminal.label: terminal memory leak resolved

question_patterns: What version is the scheduler running?

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The affected cluster runs v1.30.4 rather than v1.30.3.

question_patterns: Is SchedulerQueueingHints enabled when this happens?
Does the scheduler actually OOM with QueueingHint enabled?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, QueueingHint is enabled, and the scheduler eventually OOMs.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: QueueingHint has never been enabled on this cluster; the scheduler OOMs in the default configuration.

question_patterns: What happens if you disable the QueueingHint feature gate?
Can you compare scheduler memory with the feature enabled and disabled?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: After I disabled the QueueingHint feature gate, the scheduler stopped OOMing. These are the memory graphs from before and after disabling it.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Disabling QueueingHint makes no difference; memory grows at the same rate and the scheduler still OOMs.
The graph dashboard uses a different color theme after I disable the feature.

question_patterns: Can you share a heap profile or memory data from the affected scheduler?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I captured an in-use-space heap profile from kube-scheduler and pasted its allocation table along with the before-and-after memory graphs.

edges.comment: Issue c20-c24, participant6's cluster: the affected operator supplies the v1.30.3 reproduction, heap data, and enabled/disabled comparison. This second affected participant is folded into the simulated user side; the feature-gate change is treated as a diagnostic configuration probe.

question_patterns: Can you provide a pprof call graph or flame graph from the affected scheduler?
Do you have more detailed profiling output than the allocation table?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, I reproduced it in this cluster and captured these pprof graph views.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The profile is dominated by an unrelated custom scheduler plugin, with no substantial allocation path through event watching or the scheduling queue.
I captured the same graph from a second five-minute profile and it has the same large paths.

question_patterns: Is the scheduler still scheduling Pods while memory is high, or has scheduling stopped?
Do new Pods continue to get scheduled during the growth?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It is still scheduling Pods while the memory is growing.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: No Pods are scheduled once the growth starts; every scheduling worker is blocked.

edges.comment: Issue c25-c30, participant6's system: the operator supplies pprof images and confirms scheduling continues. The reporter's later interpretation that watching consumes substantial memory is engineer-side and is not placed in the user's answer.

question_patterns: Can you log the current sizes of inFlightPods and inFlightEvents while memory grows?
Please add temporary queue-size logging and paste the raw counts.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I added the debug log. The output repeatedly has only two to five inFlightPods, while inFlightEvents is already around 62,741 and higher.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both values remain proportional: about five inFlightPods and five inFlightEvents, even as process memory grows.
The run starts near 58,000 events rather than 62,000, with the same two-to-five in-flight Pods.

question_patterns: Do the event counts remain stable, or do they continue increasing across the log?
What is the raw trend in inFlightEvents?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The inFlightEvents number keeps rising on successive lines: 62741, 62747, 62753, 62765, 62766, 62768, 62773, 62774, 62779 and onward.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The event count falls back to zero whenever the last in-flight Pod completes.

edges.comment: Issue c34-c36, participant6's cluster: handler-requested instrumentation produces raw queue-size logs. The answer deliberately reports only counts and trend; concluding which queue invariant is broken remains engineer inference.

solution.intent: Unconditionally defer SchedulingQueue.Done for every Pod at the start of ScheduleOne so in-flight entries are removed immediately.
solution.concrete_example: Add `defer sched.SchedulingQueue.Done(pod.UID)` immediately after obtaining the Pod in ScheduleOne.
solution.inference_hint: Although the diagnostic code keeps the measured counters low, the maintainer rejects it because a Pod entering the binding cycle must remain represented until binding completes; ScheduleOne cannot call Done unconditionally.

edges.comment: Issue c38-c39, participant6's temporary code probe and the reporter's rejection. The probe visibly reduces the counters, but it violates binding-cycle lifetime semantics and is not a valid fix. It is modeled as a throwaway diagnostic patch, so the persistent system state does not change.

question_patterns: Please restore the original ScheduleOne code, test one of the proposed candidate builds, and report whether the original problem still occurs.
Can you cherry-pick one of the proposed candidate patches and retry the affected workload?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I cherry-picked the proposed change and tried again. The problem is solved by the multi-element-in-the-list change.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The scheduler still accumulates events and OOMs after I test the proposed patch.
The same change solves it after a second restart of the test scheduler.

edges.comment: Issue c41-c43, participant6's affected cluster: the reporter asks for a candidate-patch test, and the operator reports that the multi-element list change solves the problem. This is pre-landing candidate verification and therefore remains a clarification measurement.

solution.intent: Make in-flight tracking robust to the same Pod having multiple list entries, so completion removes the correct entries and no orphan can indefinitely retain subsequent events; retain regression coverage that monitors in-flight event growth.
solution.concrete_example: Track all in-flight list elements associated with a Pod UID rather than overwriting a single map pointer. When the Pod is done, clean up the applicable elements without ending its binding-cycle lifetime early, and exercise the queue under scheduler_perf while checking the in-flight-events metric.
solution.inference_hint: The raw logs only establish that a handful of in-flight Pods coexist with a monotonically growing event list. The maintainer derives the final mechanism: on the affected version, one Pod can be popped again while an earlier scheduling/binding cycle is active; the list then contains multiple entries for that UID, while the map retains only the newest element. Done removes that newer element, leaving the older element to pin all later events. The affected operator's multi-element-patch result validates this inference.

edges.comment: Final diagnosis and resolution from c40-c47. The reporter identifies the duplicate-Pop/list-versus-map failure, the affected operator verifies the robust multi-element change, and later scheduler_perf coverage is added to detect equivalent retention. Bot closure and assignment logistics are omitted.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: the same Pod can have multiple in-flight list entries, but a single map entry is overwritten to point only to the newest element; Done then removes only that element and leaves an older entry that prevents accumulated events from being cleaned.

Must ground the diagnosis in the collected evidence: QueueingHint-dependent OOM behavior, very few in-flight Pods alongside more than 62,000 monotonically increasing inFlightEvents, and successful testing of the multi-element list change.
Must not recommend unconditionally calling SchedulingQueue.Done at the start of ScheduleOne; that diagnostic probe breaks the required lifetime of Pods that enter the binding cycle.
The durable fix must correctly account for multiple in-flight elements per Pod and include metric-based scheduler_perf regression coverage for excessive in-flight event growth.
Must treat the issue as resolved only after an affected operator verifies that a build containing the robust queue change no longer exhibits the memory problem.

persona_hint.experience_level: Kubernetes scheduler maintainer combined with an experienced affected cluster operator: comfortable building scheduler patches, collecting pprof data, adding Go debug logs, changing feature gates, and cherry-picking candidate fixes.
persona_hint.communication_style: Technical and collaborative; shares raw profiles and log excerpts, answers direct diagnostic questions concisely, and distinguishes observations from uncertainty about the underlying cause.
